name: Guillotine Escape to Von Flue
description: Master the Guillotine Escape to Von Flue choke in BJJ. Complete guide to countering bottom guillotine attempts with shoulder pressure from side control.
summary: The Guillotine Escape to Von Flue is a counter to a bottom-guard guillotine in which the trapped top player passes toward the choking-arm side and drives shoulder pressure into the exposed carotid, weaponizing the opponent's own grip into a Von Flue choke.
overview:
The Guillotine Escape to Von Flue is one of the most elegant counter-techniques in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, transforming a defensive survival situation into an offensive submission opportunity. When caught in a guillotine from the bottom player's guard, the top player methodically passes to side control on the choking arm side. If the bottom player stubbornly maintains their guillotine grip after the pass is completed, they inadvertently create the conditions for their own demise—the Von Flue choke. The top player drives shoulder pressure directly into the carotid artery on the side held open by the opponent's extended neck, using their own grip structure against them.

This technique exemplifies the principle of turning defensive liability into offensive advantage. Rather than fighting to strip the guillotine grip—which burns energy and often fails—the practitioner accepts the grip and redirects the engagement into a passing sequence. The Von Flue choke works precisely because the opponent maintains their guillotine hold: their own arm compresses one side of the neck while your shoulder compresses the other. This bilateral compression creates a blood choke that can render opponents unconscious in seconds. The technique has become a staple counter at all competitive levels after numerous high-profile finishes demonstrated its reliability.

Strategically, the mere threat of the Von Flue forces guillotine players to reconsider holding their grip once the guard is passed. This creates a powerful deterrent effect—experienced practitioners who know the Von Flue will release their guillotine early during guard passing attempts, which itself benefits the passer by removing the choking threat and conceding side control. The technique functions both as a direct submission counter and as a strategic tool that shapes opponent behavior, making it invaluable for anyone who regularly faces guillotine attacks from bottom guard.
conditions: Opponent is holding a guillotine choke grip from bottom guard position
You are the top player with your head trapped in the guillotine
Your head is positioned on the same side as the opponent's choking arm
Opponent's guard can be opened or bypassed through lateral passing
You can maintain consciousness long enough to complete the guard passing sequence

variants_and_adaptations.description: Rapid lateral pass to side control before opponent can adjust grip or finish the choke. Prioritizes passing speed over weight distribution during the transition, relying on explosive movement to reach side control before the guillotine takes effect.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the guillotine pressure is tight and you need to reach side control quickly before the choke takes effect or the opponent can adjust to a more dangerous variation.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Slow, grinding pass using heavy shoulder pressure and methodical weight distribution to neutralize the guillotine while transitioning to side control. Each step consolidates position before advancing, reducing the choking pressure incrementally throughout the pass.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the guillotine pressure is manageable and you have time to establish dominant positioning throughout the pass without risking being finished during the transition.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Applying Von Flue shoulder pressure from half guard top when the opponent catches a guillotine. You drive your shoulder into their neck while their own half guard legs prevent them from creating the space needed to relieve the pressure or release the grip effectively.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you are caught in a guillotine from half guard bottom and can drive your shoulder into their neck without needing to fully pass guard first.

position_integration: The Guillotine Escape to Von Flue occupies a critical junction in the BJJ positional hierarchy, connecting the front headlock and guillotine control system to the side control submission ecosystem. It serves as the primary deterrent against bottom guillotine attempts, punishing opponents who hold the grip after guard passes are completed. This technique integrates seamlessly with standard guard passing methodology—the passing mechanics are identical to normal guillotine defense, with the Von Flue adding a submission layer on top. Practitioners who develop this counter fundamentally change the risk calculus for guillotine attackers, creating a deterrent effect that extends beyond the specific technique encounter and influences the entire front headlock exchange dynamic.

attacker.name: Guillotine Escape to Von Flue Attacker
attacker.description: Execute the Guillotine Escape to Von Flue choke. Step-by-step guide to escaping bottom guillotine and countering with shoulder pressure submission from side control.
attacker.overview: As the attacker in the Guillotine Escape to Von Flue, you are the practitioner caught in a guillotine from the bottom player's guard who transforms this defensive crisis into a submission opportunity. Your objective is to methodically pass to side control on the choking arm side while your opponent maintains their guillotine grip. Once you establish side control, your shoulder drives directly into the exposed side of their neck—the same side their own arm is compressing from the opposite direction. This bilateral compression creates an extremely efficient blood choke that can produce unconsciousness within seconds. The technique demands precise understanding of passing angles, shoulder placement, and composure under pressure, as you must remain calm while being actively choked during the initial passing phase. Mastery of this counter fundamentally changes how opponents approach guillotine attacks against you, creating a deterrent that improves your entire front headlock defense.
key_principles: Pass to the choking arm side exclusively—this is the only side where Von Flue choke mechanics function, as your shoulder must compress the carotid opposite the opponent's forearm
Maintain forward pressure throughout the guard pass to prevent opponent from adjusting their grip, switching variations, or re-establishing guard structure
Drive your shoulder into the opponent's neck at the carotid artery below the jaw line, not into the chest or chin, targeting the soft tissue between jaw and collarbone
Keep your hips low and sprawled once in side control to prevent guard recovery and maximize the gravitational force channeled through your shoulder
Exercise patience once shoulder pressure is established—the Von Flue works through sustained pressure rather than explosive squeezing, and the choke effect is cumulative
Control the opponent's free arm to prevent framing that could create space and relieve the bilateral compression on their neck
setup_requirements: Opponent has an active guillotine grip from bottom guard position with committed head control
You can create enough posture through chin tuck and partial extension to begin a lateral passing sequence despite the choke
Your head is positioned on the same side as the opponent's choking arm, which is required for Von Flue mechanics
Opponent is committed to maintaining the guillotine grip rather than transitioning to alternative attacks or releasing
You have identified or can create a pathway to clear the opponent's legs and pass guard laterally

execution_steps.description: Tuck your chin tightly against the opponent's chest to reduce choking pressure on your trachea. Create just enough posture to begin moving laterally without fully breaking their grip. Focus on protecting the airway while preparing to pass—the chin tuck buys critical seconds during the transition.

execution_steps.action: Walk hips toward the choking arm side
execution_steps.description: Begin lateral movement by walking your hips and feet toward the side where the opponent's choking arm is positioned. This direction is absolutely critical—passing to the wrong side eliminates the Von Flue possibility entirely. Use small, controlled steps while maintaining your chin tuck and forward pressure.

execution_steps.action: Clear opponent's legs and pass guard
execution_steps.description: Use your nearside arm to control the opponent's hip and prevent guard retention while your hips drive past their legs. Push their top knee down with your hand or forearm as you step over their thigh. Speed matters during this phase—the longer you take, the more time the guillotine choke has to work against you.

Once past the guard, immediately drive your shoulder into the side of the opponent's neck at the carotid artery below the jaw line. Your shoulder should press into the side that their own choking arm is not compressing—this creates bilateral neck compression using their guillotine grip structure against them.

execution_steps.action: Sprawl hips and settle body weight
execution_steps.description: Sprawl your hips back and drive your weight downward through your shoulder into the opponent's neck. Your body should form an angle where gravity amplifies the shoulder pressure naturally. Keep your hips low and heavy against the mat to prevent any guard recovery attempts and seal the position.

Use your nearside arm to control the opponent's free arm—the one not involved in the guillotine grip—by pinning it to the mat or securing an underhook. This prevents them from framing against your hip or shoulder to create space that would relieve the bilateral choking pressure.

execution_steps.action: Maintain pressure and wait for resolution
execution_steps.description: Hold the position with consistent, heavy shoulder pressure through skeletal alignment rather than muscular effort. The opponent faces a binary choice: maintain the guillotine grip and be choked unconscious by the Von Flue, or release the grip and concede side control. Either outcome is favorable for you.

common_counters.counter: Opponent releases guillotine grip before Von Flue is established and immediately frames for guard recovery
common_counters.your_response: Immediately consolidate side control with crossface and hip control before they can create distance. Their grip release removes the Von Flue opportunity but gives you dominant side control position—transition to standard top attacks.

common_counters.counter: Opponent closes guard tightly around your waist to prevent the lateral passing sequence
common_counters.your_response: Use standard guard opening techniques—drive knee into their tailbone, posture with both hands on their hips, and work to create the space needed to resume the lateral pass. The Von Flue requires passing their guard first.

common_counters.counter: Opponent transitions to high elbow guillotine during your pass attempt, increasing choke danger
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate the passing speed and commit fully to reaching side control. The high elbow guillotine is more dangerous but requires specific body positioning that becomes harder to maintain as you drive laterally past their guard legs.

common_counters.counter: Opponent swings legs up for high guard or triangle configuration to prevent lateral pass completion
common_counters.your_response: Posture hard and drive your trapped arm elbow toward their hip to break the high guard angle. Use your free arm to push their leg off your shoulder before they can lock the triangle position.

common_errors.error: Passing to the wrong side, away from the choking arm
common_errors.consequence: Von Flue mechanics cannot work because your shoulder is on the wrong side of their neck—you end up in side control with no submission threat while having endured the guillotine choke during the entire passing sequence
common_errors.correction: Always identify which arm is the choking arm before initiating the pass. Your shoulder must press into the side of the neck opposite from where the opponent's forearm compresses—this requires passing toward the choking arm.

common_errors.error: Attempting to strip the guillotine grip before passing guard
common_errors.consequence: Burns significant energy fighting their grip while remaining trapped in their guard, allowing them to adjust grip depth and increase choking pressure or transition to more dangerous variations
common_errors.correction: Accept the grip and focus entirely on passing. The grip becomes your weapon once you achieve side control—grip stripping attempts are wasteful when the lateral pass itself is the optimal solution.

common_errors.error: Shoulder positioned too high on the jaw or chin instead of on the neck
common_errors.consequence: Causes discomfort and jaw pressure but does not create effective blood choke on the carotid artery, allowing opponent to survive indefinitely and eventually escape or adjust their grip
common_errors.correction: Drive your shoulder into the soft tissue of the neck below the jaw line, directly over the carotid artery. The correct pressure point is between the jaw and the collarbone where blood flow is most vulnerable.

common_errors.error: Hips too high during side control, leaving space underneath the body
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses the space to insert a knee, recover half guard or full guard, and escape the Von Flue position entirely while potentially re-establishing the guillotine threat
common_errors.correction: Sprawl your hips back and keep them heavy against the mat. Your body should function like a weighted plank driving shoulder pressure downward through gravity and structural alignment rather than muscular effort.

common_errors.error: Rushing through the pass and arriving in side control with poor shoulder placement
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the failed pressure placement and releases their guillotine grip during your positional adjustment, escaping the Von Flue window without consequence and leaving you to work from standard side control
common_errors.correction: As you pass, deliberately place your shoulder on their neck before fully settling into side control. The transition from guard pass to Von Flue pressure must be seamless—not a two-step process.

common_errors.error: Panicking due to active guillotine pressure and abandoning the pass attempt entirely
common_errors.consequence: Remain stuck in opponent's guard with an active guillotine choke, burning energy and oxygen defending while they maintain the attacking position and continue squeezing
common_errors.correction: Stay calm and trust the technique. Tuck your chin firmly, protect the airway, and continue the passing sequence methodically. Choking pressure decreases significantly once you begin clearing the guard and your weight shifts laterally.

training_progressions.description: Practice establishing Von Flue shoulder pressure from side control with a cooperative partner who holds a loose guillotine grip. Focus on finding the exact shoulder position that creates carotid compression. No resistance—pure positional awareness and anatomical understanding.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Guard Passing Under Choke Pressure
training_progressions.focus: Completing the lateral pass while being guillotined
training_progressions.description: Partner applies moderate guillotine pressure while you practice the lateral passing sequence to the choking arm side. Focus on chin tuck, posture management, and timing of the pass. Partner increases guillotine intensity progressively across rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Connecting the escape to the choke as one fluid movement
training_progressions.description: Combine the guard pass and Von Flue setup into a single continuous sequence. Partner applies full guillotine pressure and defends the pass at 70% resistance. Develop timing and confidence in committing to the pass while being actively choked.

Positional sparring starting from guillotine control bottom. Both players work at full intensity—bottom player attempts to finish guillotine or transition to alternative attacks, top player works the Von Flue counter or escapes. Develop pattern recognition and commitment timing.

training_progressions.focus: Responding to opponent's defensive adjustments dynamically
training_progressions.description: Partner varies their defense between maintaining grip, releasing early, switching to high elbow, and closing guard tightly. Practice reading each response and adjusting—consolidate side control on grip release, re-open guard on closure, accelerate pass on high elbow switch.

flashcards.question: What side must you pass to when executing the Guillotine Escape to Von Flue?
flashcards.answer: You must pass to the choking arm side—the side where the opponent's forearm crosses your neck. This positions your shoulder against the carotid artery on the side opposite from where their arm compresses, creating bilateral neck compression. Passing to the wrong side eliminates the Von Flue opportunity entirely and wastes the passing effort.
flashcards.answer_line: Pass to the choking arm side

plausible: Pass away from the choking arm
Pass to whichever side is open
trap: Stay in guard and strip the grip

flashcards.question: Your opponent has a tight guillotine from closed guard and you cannot open their legs—what must you address first?
flashcards.answer: You must open their closed guard before the lateral pass is possible. Drive your knee into their tailbone, posture up while maintaining a firm chin tuck to protect the airway, and use standard guard-opening techniques with hand positioning on their hips. The Von Flue is only available once you can pass the guard, so guard opening is the essential prerequisite step.

plausible: Posture up to break the choke
trap: Force the pass through locked legs

flashcards.question: Where exactly should your shoulder be positioned to create effective Von Flue choke pressure?
flashcards.answer: Your shoulder should press into the soft tissue of the neck between the jaw line and the collarbone, directly over the carotid artery. Too high on the jaw creates discomfort without blood flow restriction. Too low on the chest creates no choking pressure whatsoever. The correct placement causes immediate narrowing of blood flow to the brain.

plausible: High up on the jaw line

flashcards.question: Your opponent releases the guillotine grip as you begin establishing side control—what is your immediate response?
flashcards.answer: Immediately abandon the Von Flue attempt and consolidate standard side control with crossface and hip control. Their grip release means you have successfully escaped the guillotine and achieved a dominant position. Establish heavy crossface pressure, block their far hip, and begin working standard side control submissions and transitions.

plausible: Keep hunting for Von Flue pressure

flashcards.question: What is the most critical mechanical detail during the guard passing phase of this technique?
flashcards.answer: Maintaining your chin tucked tightly against the opponent's chest throughout the entire pass is the single most critical detail. The chin tuck protects your trachea from the most dangerous direct choking pressure while you complete the lateral passing movement. Without the chin tuck, the guillotine can finish you during the vulnerable passing phase.

plausible: Chin tucked to your own chest
trap: Turn head away from the choke

flashcards.question: How do you prevent the opponent from recovering guard once you establish side control with Von Flue shoulder pressure?
flashcards.answer: Keep your hips sprawled back and heavy with your weight driving downward through your shoulder using gravity and skeletal alignment. Use your nearside arm to block their far hip, preventing any knee insertion for guard recovery. Your body should create a complete seal against their torso with zero space for their legs to work between your bodies.
flashcards.answer_line: Sprawl hips, block their far hip

plausible: Sit up tall for more weight
trap: Post both hands on the mat

flashcards.question: Your opponent switches to a high elbow guillotine as you begin passing—how does this change your approach?
flashcards.answer: Accelerate your passing speed immediately and commit fully to reaching side control. The high elbow guillotine is significantly more dangerous than the standard variation, but maintaining its specific mechanics becomes very difficult as you drive laterally past their guard. The increased danger makes decisive, rapid action more important than methodical passing.

plausible: Stop and strip the elbow grip

flashcards.question: The Von Flue choke is not producing a tap and your opponent appears comfortable—what adjustments should you make to the direction of force?
flashcards.answer: Angle your shoulder pressure slightly forward toward the mat rather than straight down, driving the point of your shoulder deeper into the carotid. Walk your hips further behind you to increase the gravitational component through your shoulder. You can also micro-adjust by turning your head toward their hips, which rotates the shoulder bone and changes the pressure angle on the artery. The force must compress the carotid laterally, not push into the trachea.
flashcards.answer_line: Angle shoulder down, walk hips back

plausible: Turn head away from their hips
trap: Drive the shoulder into the trachea

flashcards.question: Your opponent successfully defends the Von Flue by releasing the grip but you cannot consolidate side control before they start framing—what chain attacks are available?
flashcards.answer: Immediately transition to standard side control attacks exploiting their compromised position. Their near arm is likely out of position from releasing the guillotine, making it vulnerable to Americana or kimura. If they turn into you while framing, threaten arm triangle or darce choke. If they bridge away, follow to knee on belly. The key is recognizing that escaping the guillotine and achieving any form of top control is already a significant win—chain to whatever their defensive reaction exposes.

flashcards.question: What specific grip or hand positioning do you use with your free arm during the guard passing phase of this technique?
flashcards.answer: Your free arm—the one not trapped in the guillotine—controls the opponent's hip on the choking arm side by pushing their knee or thigh down and away. This hand drives into their hip crease or pushes their top knee to the mat to clear the passing path. Once past the guard, this arm transitions to controlling their far arm or underhooking to prevent framing. The free hand never reaches for their choking arm grip—it stays focused on hip control and leg clearing throughout the pass.

plausible: Underhook the far arm right away

attacker.safety_considerations: The Von Flue choke is a blood choke that can produce unconsciousness within seconds once properly established. Always tap immediately when caught in a Von Flue during training—the onset of unconsciousness is often sudden without gradual warning sensations. When applying the technique, maintain constant awareness of your partner's consciousness and release immediately upon tap or any signs of distress. During the passing phase, practitioners should tap early if the guillotine is too tight to survive the passing sequence rather than risking oxygen deprivation or cervical injury. Never ignore neck pain symptoms—cervical spine compression can occur if excessive downward shoulder force is applied improperly.

defender.name: Guillotine Escape to Von Flue Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Von Flue choke counter to your guillotine. Recognition cues, grip release timing, and guard retention strategies to avoid being submitted by your own grip.
defender.overview: As the defender in the Guillotine Escape to Von Flue scenario, you are the practitioner who initiated the guillotine attack from bottom guard and must now prevent your own grip from being weaponized against you. The critical defensive challenge is recognizing when your opponent begins passing toward your choking arm side—this is the moment your guillotine transitions from offensive weapon to defensive liability. Your primary defensive tools are guard retention to prevent the pass entirely, early grip release to abandon the guillotine before the Von Flue becomes possible, and grip adjustment to switch to higher-percentage guillotine variations that maintain the submission threat even during partial guard passing. Understanding the Von Flue counter fundamentally changes how you should approach guillotine attacks from bottom position—the guillotine is only safe while your guard integrity prevents the pass.
key_principles: Recognize when your opponent begins passing toward your choking arm side—this directional change is the critical signal that Von Flue is being set up
Release the guillotine grip proactively when the guard pass becomes imminent rather than stubbornly holding and exposing yourself to bilateral neck compression
Use your legs actively to prevent the guard pass—close your guard, establish butterfly hooks, or create shin frames specifically on the choking arm side
If maintaining the guillotine, adjust to high elbow variation which offers better finishing mechanics and makes the opponent's lateral pass more difficult to complete
Monitor your own neck exposure continuously—once you feel shoulder pressure settling on your neck from side control, release the grip immediately without hesitation
Frame with your free arm against the opponent's hip to create space and prevent them from settling full weight into the Von Flue shoulder pressure position
recognition_cues: Opponent tucks chin and begins walking hips laterally toward your choking arm side instead of trying to posture up or strip your grip
Opponent stops attempting to break your guillotine grip and instead redirects all effort toward passing your guard laterally
Feeling opponent's weight shifting perpendicular to your body as they transition from inside your guard to beside you
Opponent's shoulder begins pressing into the side of your neck as they clear your legs during the guard pass
Your choking arm begins compressing your own neck against the opponent's shoulder from the opposite side—bilateral pressure sensation

defensive_options.action: Release guillotine grip immediately and frame for guard recovery using both arms
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as opponent begins clearing your guard legs while passing to the choking arm side and you cannot prevent the pass
defensive_options.if_successful: You recover to open guard in a neutral position, avoiding the Von Flue entirely and retaining defensive guard structure for continued play
defensive_options.risk: If you release too late, opponent may already have established side control with shoulder pressure and you lose both the guillotine and guard position

defensive_options.action: Close guard tightly around opponent's waist and increase guillotine pressure to finish before pass completes
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you detect the pass attempt early and still have your legs wrapped around the opponent's waist with full guard closure
defensive_options.if_successful: You maintain guillotine control in closed guard and continue attacking the submission with full leverage and control
defensive_options.risk: If the guillotine does not finish and the opponent forces your guard open, you may end up in Von Flue position with less reaction time

defensive_options.action: Switch to high elbow guillotine and angle your body to prevent the lateral passing sequence
defensive_options.when_to_use: When opponent begins posturing and you can feel them initiating the lateral pass but your guard still has partial integrity
defensive_options.if_successful: High elbow guillotine maintains a stronger choking angle that is significantly harder for the passer to survive during the transition
defensive_options.risk: The grip adjustment creates a brief window during which the opponent can accelerate the pass and bypass your guard entirely

defensive_options.action: Hip escape away from the pass direction and re-establish guard hooks before opponent clears legs
defensive_options.when_to_use: When opponent has begun passing but has not yet fully cleared your legs from the passing path
defensive_options.if_successful: You create distance and recover to open guard or half guard with your control reestablished and the guillotine threat neutralized safely
defensive_options.risk: Hip escaping may compromise your guillotine grip position and the opponent can follow your movement to complete the pass

favorable_outcomes.how: Prevent the guard pass entirely by closing your guard tightly, maintaining active hip positioning, and either finishing the guillotine choke or transitioning to a higher-percentage variation like the high elbow guillotine before the opponent can establish side control.

Release the guillotine grip early when you recognize the Von Flue setup developing, immediately frame with both arms against the opponent's shoulders and hips to create distance, and use hip escape movement to re-establish open guard before the opponent can consolidate side control.

common_errors.error: Holding guillotine grip stubbornly after opponent has passed to side control
common_errors.consequence: Your own arm becomes an integral part of the Von Flue choke mechanism—your forearm compresses one side of your neck while the opponent's shoulder compresses the other side, creating rapid bilateral blood choke
common_errors.correction: Release the guillotine immediately when you feel the opponent's shoulder settle on your neck from side control. Use that arm to frame against their shoulder or hip to begin standard side control escape sequences instead.

common_errors.error: Neglecting leg activity and allowing a free guard pass while focused entirely on the guillotine finish
common_errors.consequence: Opponent passes to side control unchallenged, establishing ideal Von Flue shoulder positioning with maximum time to settle weight and secure the choke before you can react
common_errors.correction: Maintain active legs throughout the guillotine attack at all times. Even while squeezing the choke with maximum effort, your legs must prevent the pass through closed guard, butterfly hooks, or shin frames.

common_errors.error: Attempting to bridge into the shoulder pressure when Von Flue is being applied
common_errors.consequence: Bridging drives your own neck harder into the opponent's shoulder, actually increasing the bilateral blood choke pressure and accelerating the path to unconsciousness
common_errors.correction: If the Von Flue is being applied, do not bridge toward the shoulder. Instead release the grip immediately, turn your head away from the shoulder pressure, and frame against the opponent's hip to create escape space.

common_errors.error: Adjusting guillotine grip configuration without simultaneously maintaining guard integrity
common_errors.consequence: The momentary loosening of control during the grip transition gives the opponent a clear window to accelerate the lateral pass and establish side control before the new grip is secured
common_errors.correction: Any grip adjustment must be paired with increased leg activity—close your guard tighter or insert a butterfly hook before switching between grip configurations to prevent exploitation of the transition window.

flashcards.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that your opponent is setting up a Von Flue counter to your guillotine?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cue is when your opponent stops trying to strip your guillotine grip and instead begins walking their hips laterally toward your choking arm side. This directional change indicates they have accepted your grip and plan to weaponize it against you. Most practitioners instinctively try to strip the grip first, so the shift to pass-focused lateral movement is the critical warning signal.

trap: They pull your head down harder

flashcards.question: You are holding a guillotine from closed guard and feel your opponent's shoulder pressing into your neck—what should you do immediately?
flashcards.answer: Release the guillotine grip immediately without hesitation—the Von Flue choke is already in progress and every second you maintain the grip increases the bilateral compression on your neck. After releasing, use both arms to frame against the opponent's shoulders and hips, turn your head away from the shoulder pressure, and begin working standard side control bottom escape sequences.

plausible: Hold the grip and wait it out

flashcards.question: How does understanding the Von Flue counter change your overall approach to guillotine attacks from bottom guard?
flashcards.answer: Understanding the Von Flue counter means you must always monitor your guard integrity simultaneously with your choke progress. The guillotine is only safe while your guard prevents the lateral pass. If you sense the guard weakening, you must either finish the choke immediately or release and recover guard rather than stubbornly holding a compromised grip that could be turned into a weapon against you.
flashcards.answer_line: Finish fast or bail and reguard

plausible: Stall in guard until they tire
trap: Crank the choke as they pass

flashcards.question: What leg positioning best prevents the lateral guard pass that enables the Von Flue setup?
flashcards.answer: Closed guard with legs locked high on the opponent's back provides the strongest prevention against the lateral pass required for Von Flue. If closed guard is not possible, a butterfly hook on the choking arm side combined with an overhook prevents lateral movement in that critical direction. Your legs must create barriers specifically on the choking arm side where the Von Flue requires the pass.
flashcards.answer_line: Lock legs high, block choke side

trap: Open guard for a better angle

flashcards.question: What should your free arm be doing while you hold the guillotine to prevent the Von Flue counter?
flashcards.answer: Your free arm—the one reinforcing the choke or controlling the opponent's body—should actively block the opponent's hip on the choking arm side to prevent their lateral movement. If they begin walking their hips, use your free arm as a frame against their shoulder on the passing side to stall the pass. This arm is your early warning system and first line of defense against the lateral pass that enables the Von Flue.
flashcards.answer_line: Block hip on choking arm side

plausible: Push on their head to posture
trap: Post it on the mat for base

flashcards.question: You are attacking a guillotine from butterfly guard and your opponent begins passing laterally—why is this more dangerous than from closed guard and how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Butterfly guard provides less lateral pass prevention than closed guard because butterfly hooks primarily resist forward and upward movement, not lateral passing. When you feel the lateral pass beginning from butterfly, you must either immediately close your guard around their waist to lock them in place, or release the guillotine and use your butterfly hooks to elevate and create distance for guard recovery. The open nature of butterfly guard means the window between pass initiation and Von Flue danger is much shorter than from closed guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Close guard or release and hook

plausible: Hold the grip and wait for a tap
Switch hooks to attack the back
trap: Post both hands on the mat

training_progressions.focus: Identifying Von Flue setup cues versus standard guillotine defense
training_progressions.description: Partner alternates between standard guillotine defense responses (grip stripping, posturing) and Von Flue setup movements (lateral passing). Practice identifying which approach the opponent is taking and making the correct defensive decision—maintain guillotine against grip stripping, prepare to release against lateral passing.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Release Timing and Guard Recovery
training_progressions.focus: Developing the grip release to guard recovery sequence
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts Von Flue passing sequence at progressive resistance levels. Practice the critical decision point of when to release the guillotine and transition immediately to guard recovery framing and hip escape. Develop the muscle memory for the release-to-frame-to-escape sequence as one continuous movement.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining guard while attacking guillotine simultaneously
training_progressions.description: Full positional sparring from guillotine control bottom position. Practice keeping your guard intact and legs active while simultaneously working the guillotine finish. training_progressions.focus: Finishing guillotine before Von Flue completes
training_progressions.description: Partner commits to the Von Flue passing sequence at full intensity. Practice finishing the guillotine during the opponent's passing attempt by exploiting their forward momentum and timing the maximum choke pressure as they drive through the pass. This is advanced timing work requiring excellent feel.
